catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q1.explanation: C - evenIt is used here to highlight a surprising or extreme possibility—that singing might have been a form of communication for Neanderthals.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q2.explanation: B - resulted‘Resulted from’ is the best collocation here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q3.explanation: D - occupiedResided and dwelt would need the ‘in’ preposition. Filled implies that they were very numerous, which isn’t stated in the text. Occupied is more neutral.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q4.explanation: B - assumed‘To assume’ means to take for granted and without any actual proof. As the context suggest, previous beliefs about Neanderthal voices had no scientific ground.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q5.explanation: D - formAnother set expression. The other possible option is approach to communication, albeit with a different preposition so it can’t be used here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q6.explanation: A - coincides‘To coincide with’ means ‘to take place at the same time, simultaneously’. Co-operate is the only other verb that can be followed by ‘with’, but the text speaks of no cooperation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q7.explanation: A - differedAgain, the only verb that collocates with ‘from’ preposition here. ‘Markedly’ here means ‘noticeable, distinguishable, easy to see’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-1-q8.explanation: build Build refers to a person’s or animal’s physical form and size.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-2-q10.explanation: in/into‘To pop in/into’ means to visit the place briefly, for a short time.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-2-q12.explanation: well‘As well as’ = in addition to. ‘We went shopping to buy some groceries as well as today’s newspaper’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-2-q13.explanation: get‘To get someone hooked on something’ = to involve someone in something, to allure someone to do something, usually addictive (like reading, sports, substances).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-2-q14.explanation: forWe normally use the ‘for’ preposition with ordinal numbers (first, second, third and so on).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-2-q15.explanation: aThe indefinite article is used here because we are not talking about any particular selection of books, and it is mentioned for the first time in this text. See articles page for more information.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-2-q16.explanation: withWe cannot use ‘and’ here because there is no ‘is’ before ‘being’ in the last sentence. Therefore ‘with’ is the only option that fits.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q17.explanation: originallyOriginally means ‘in the first place’. The context demands an adverb to be used here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q18.explanation: sight‘At first sight’ means ‘from the start, from the beginning’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q19.explanation: untrainedIt is suggested by contest that we should use negative prefix ‘un-‘. The second part of the sentence makes it clear.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q20.explanation: workoutA workout is any exercise aimed at developing your body. Don’t forget that you can’t leave the word unchanged, even though ‘work’ would fit grammatically.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q21.explanation: necessarilyAn adverb is needed here. Pay attention to spelling, it is easy to make a mistake and not get a point for this answer.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q22.explanation: A verb is needed. AmE spelling is ‘maximize’, it won’t be regarded as a mistake if you spell it that way, but BrE spelling is preferable. The general guideline for Cambridge exams is to be consistent with your choice – so stick to either British or American English throughout your exam.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-3-q23.explanation: strengtheningThe preposition ‘for’ before the word says that we need to use the gerund form. Another difficult word to spell, pay attention here.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q25.explanation: come up with a solution‘To come up with’ means to produce or find something, in this case a solution (way of solving something).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q26.answer: be wondering why it has been
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q26.explanation: be wondering why it has beenPresent Perfect is used here because we have the conjunction ‘since’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q27.answer: me of not telling the truth
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q27.explanation: me of not telling the truthNote that you have to use the negative particle because the word ‘truth’ has to be used.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q28.explanation: without giving enough thought‘To give a thought to something’ means to think something over, to consider it for some time.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q29.answer: there has been a decrease in
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q29.explanation: there has been a decrease inNote that decrease here should be used as a noun rather than a verb.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q30.answer: however bad his behaviour OR however badly behaved he.
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-4-q30.explanation: however bad his behaviour OR however badly(-)behaved he‘However bad/badly’ means ‘no matter how bad/badly’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-5-q31.explanation: AAnswer B is incorrect — the process is well understood and is described in detail in the second paragraph. It is the cause of the process that isn’t clear. Answer C is not mentioned. Answer D is wrong because how long the debate was isn’t stated in the first two paragraphs. ‘For decades’ in sentence four refers to the information given in textbooks, not debates.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-5-q32.explanation: BBy‘the opposite purposes’ the authors compare Hamilton’s earlier study about birds who use their bright feathers to attract females. Trees on the other hand use colourful leaves to discourage insects from choosing it. Answers A and C are not mentioned. There is nothing about increased survival rate of trees mentioned in answer D.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-5-q33.explanation: AMost of paragraph 3 is about how bright leaves allow trees to protect themselves from harmful insects. Colourful leaves act as a warning sign to insects. Answer B isn’t mentioned — there is nothing said about reduction in numbers of certain insects. Proximity of insects mentioned in Answer C isn’t stated. No other defence mechanisms are talked about, so answer D is wrong as well.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-5-q34.explanation: D‘It was a first stab to see what was out there’ means that he didn’t aim to gain any conclusive information on the subject. ‘Stab’ is a colloquial term for ‘attempt, try’. Answer B is wrong — Archetti’s mathematical model confirmed the initial theory, which was its only aim. There is no regret mentioned in the text as answer C claims. Answer D is wrong because Archetti and Hamilton had a collaboration — they initiated the project together.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-5-q35.explanation: CThe last sentence of paragraph five states that the purpose of leaves’ colour changing mechanism is to act as a sunscreen (to protect the tree or foliage from ultraviolet rays). Answer A is wrong as the critics do not express this idea — they only give examples of certain trees that do not fit the paradigm suggested by Hamilton. Answer B is incorrect because the example with insects doesn’t describe their behaviour, but rather their period of activity. Answer D shouldn’t be chosen because no certain insects are named.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-5-q36.explanation: Brown and Archetti bring up an important question — if the sunscreen theory is correct, why don’t all trees have bright leaves? In turn, Dr. Hoch says that this question is not a ‘huge concern’. Answer B isn’t correct — it is said that the subject is worth investigating, but nothing is mentioned about the possible success of that research. Answers C and D aren’t mentioned.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-6-q37.explanation: ABoth Writer A and C are worried about companies that rely on freelance workers — because they outsource their projects to freelancers, their in-house employees become less useful as they are unfamiliar with these projects. Writer A — last sentence, Writer C — sentence two.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-6-q38.explanation: AOther writers are optimistic about growing number of freelance workers. However, Writer A believes that more freelancers drive the prices of their own services down, as some can be willing to take a job for less money to have any work at all.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-6-q39.explanation: CLast sentence of Writer B says that employed workers see freelance as ‘easy life’. Writer C concurs, saying that non-freelancers ‘envy’ self-employed people.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-6-q40.explanation: DWriters A, B and C hold that a successful freelancer is one who works hard and consistently. Writer D believes that a freelancer’s chances of success are largely based on chance (last but one sentence).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-7-q41.explanation: FThe author looks back at the years of working as a test pilot. He also mentions the unique opportunity of becoming an astronaut that he pointed out in the first paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-7-q42.explanation: E‘The situation changed’ refers to the extremely rare opportunities of joining a space flight — the topic of the previous sentence. The final part of paragraph E mentions a ‘test process’ that is then described in more detail in the following paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-7-q43.explanation: DThis paragraph is about the variety of candidates and how having certain skills and qualities may help you to be chosen for this position. The following paragraph continues this topic.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-7-q44.explanation: GThe previous paragraph mentions how getting ill in space is a difficult situation to deal with. This paragraph mentions the only possible solution to such a scenario, used as a last resort measure.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-7-q45.explanation: A‘It was also good …’ expands on the idea of remaining candidates. The selection was coming to an end, and the author was happy to learn that more than half of the group consisted of his fellow countrymen.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-7-q46.explanation: CThe last part of the previous paragraph states that there wasn’t much time left for the author to be contacted. This paragraph mentions the telephone call and how the author was excited to get the news of him being chosen for the programme.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q47.explanation: C‘what had been a largely desolate stretch’ — desolate here means ‘gloomy, depressing’. Past Perfect tense implies that it is no longer the case; the design has changed for the better.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q48.explanation: BMiddle of the paragraph starts with ‘Explaining his approach to designing …’, Paoletti compares his style to one of ‘free-form jazz’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q49.explanation: ESecond sentence of that paragraph how the design has radically transformed the appearance of the station.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q50.explanation: BPaoletti complains how the station he designed is compared to a cathedral, and he jokingly complains that it IS a cathedral, not something that looks like one.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q51.explanation: EThe last sentence of this paragraph contains Paoletti’s thoughts on the function of the underground stations.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q52.explanation: EMiddle of the same paragraph gives Paoletti’s comments on the criticism and how he managed to ‘save millions in tunnelling costs’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q53.explanation: DVery beginning of the paragraph: ‘seamless marriage of architecture and engineering’— two different elements that Paoletti attempts to unite seamlessly(without any visible transition between one and the other).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q54.explanation: ASecond sentence claims that Paoletti ‘possessed the persuasiveness and tenacity’ to accomplish this project. ‘Tenacity’ means persistence and willpower.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q55.explanation: DThird sentence mentions: ‘design stopped at the top of the escalators leading down to the platforms…’. This was as far as architects were allowed to go with their ideas.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test5-part-8-q56.explanation: AOne but last sentence contains the architect’s opinion on his predecessors:‘whom Paoletti dismissed as visionless ‘trench-diggers’’
